Leveraging the structure of the problem, we derive a closed-form solution that optimizes sum-rate beamforming for multicasting in mmWave systems with limited numbers of antennas. driving and drone operation require swift and flexible decisions, unaffected by delays. A recent advancement, Nello Nohara-Hase, has introduced a new technique leveraging a data structure called a binary forest to enhance learning speed.  Building upon this improvement, we present our own approach, Nello Forest, which offers even faster adaptation times and efficient handling of streaming data, allowing for immediate processing of new frames and rapid model creation. The model considers two types of nitrogen yields: one that depends only on a star's mass (not its metal content), which is primarily from massive stars, and another that depends on both the star's mass and metal content, which is primarily from core-collapse supernovae. Initially, we use a fixed nitrogen yield from massive stars and a linear relationship in supernovae, which is necessary to produce the observed [N/O]-[O/H] relation. environments using inverse reinforcement learning can be vulnerable to attacks through manipulated observations that alter the chosen actions and reward values. To address these limitations, we have developed a new type of attack that uses generated adversarial data to target and exploit vulnerabilities in observation data used by the IRL algorithm. To address these issues, we employ a meta-learning approach using bayesian neural networks to train and interpret a model for distinguishing between different types of magnetic excitations from a small data set. such as superconductivity, magnetism, and topological orders are frequently encountered.  Although the existence of flat bands is established in certain structures with geometric frustration like the kagome lattice, flat-band driven correlation effects are uncommon in such systems that exhibit heavy fermion behavior.  In the study presented here, the emergence of a flat band in a certain kagome metal architecture is demonstrated, and it is found that it leads to strong electronic correlations resulting in a quantum magnetic transition at a specific temperature.  The presence of a quantum metamagnetic transition at a slightly higher temperature than this value indicates that it is a spin-orbit coupled system.  The discovered metal-insulator transition and the emergence of a slightly offset Dirac point at a slightly lower temperature temperature suggest that it is a type of topological metal that exists at low temperatures.  The mechanism of a metal-insulator transition at a specific temperature can be attributed to competition between kinetically favored and locally favored ordering mechanisms.  The discovery of a flat band that drives strong electronic correlations and the presence of a topological zero-energy state in this system strongly indicates that it is a strongly correlated topological metal.

Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Yet, when compiled to Haskell, data types for qubits and other quantum elements aren't restricted, leading to a mismatch between typed Haskell code and the dynamics of quantum states. Recent research has developed a point process depth by incorporating a weighted product of two terms - one representing the depth of the process's intensity function and another accounting for the temporal fragmentation of the process. Our paper aims to address the question of whether this current definition is adequate or if further refinement is necessary. To do this, we will be focusing on the simplest form of point process data which is represented by a Poisson process, our approach will involve creating a natural metric that calculates the distance between two Poisson processes and allows for the development of a statistical depth measure. We will then investigate the applicability of this new metric in conjunction with the existing definition of depth that takes into consideration both the process's intensity function and temporal fragmentation. Through our analysis, the results suggest that the existing definition of depth is sufficient for the specific case of Poisson processes and that the proposed new metric is compatible with the existing definition. The concepts presented in this paper will be demonstrated via the use of numerical examples and accompanying software code which will allow other researchers to efficiently implement the methods described.

In this research, we explored how people use sensory information from vision and sound when identifying materials that are unfamiliar, focusing on three non-food substances (wood-foam, rubber-foam, and plastic).  Through a series of haptic experiments, participants were blindfolded and asked to feel an object while hearing a description of its visual properties.  We found that participants were able to correctly identify the material about 60% of the time when only haptic and visual information were provided.  When both visual and auditory information were available, identification accuracy increased to about 80%.  This suggests that sound provides unique information that helps people identify materials, but also indicates that vision plays a more significant role in this process.  Several high-level findings explained these results.  We then conducted a series of supplementary studies to investigate the specific role of sound in haptic perception.  These studies revealed that sound can provide valuable information about an object's material properties, but that this is largely influenced by other properties such as an object's size, texture, and weight.  Additionally, when people hear an object that differs from what was expected, they are more aware of the discrepancy and notice differences in frequency.  This research contributes to our understanding of multisensory perception and provides insights into the design of more effective haptic interfaces

Our results show that our system achieves exceptional performance in both binary and multi-class classification tasks, while also safeguarding against significant information disclosures, surpassing existing generative models in both efficacy and information security.

It has been found that the solutions exist for all values of the black hole charge, and our analysis indicates that these solutions are physically meaningful. We also numerically determined how properties of the cloud, such as mass, charge, and radial pressure, change over the course of the merger. Furthermore, our work expands on existing research by allowing for more general equations of state for the cloud and removes restrictions on its ultimate fate.

MA telescopes have revealed diverse morphologies of tidal tails in nearby galaxies, ranging from narrow and straight to broad and curved. To understand these various shapes, we developed a simplified model that accounts for multiple factors influencing tidal tails' morphology. Our model incorporates a key aspect, which is the distribution of stars within the tails, along with considerations of interactions' angles, mass of interacting galaxies, and the presence of intracluster medium. Using this model, we created artificial galaxies and performed simulations to explore different parameters' effects on tidal tails. The results show that a uniform density of stars leads to straight tidal tails, while a changing density within the tails can cause curvature. Conversely, an intracluster medium can also contribute to curvature. Additionally, dense systems tend to produce broad tidal tails, while an opposite effect occurs with weak interactions. Building on previous research, our study finds that curved tidal tails can also result from 3D hydrodynamic effects, in addition to interactions with intracluster medium.

To address this challenge, a new method was created that incorporates finite-temperature density functional theory and many-body perturbation theory to study the critical behavior of exciton condensation. involves sequences of random groupings denoted as $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$. These groupings, or partitions $\mathcal{P}_t$, split a set $\{1,2,\dots,N_t\}$ into non-empty subsets for each time point $t$. Given that $\mathcal{P}_s$ is a previous configuration at time $s$, it undergoes a transformation to $\mathcal{P}_t$ at time $t$, representing the change in groupings from $s$ to $t$. The partition process is driven by the following mechanism: at each time point, a subset from $\mathcal{P}_{t-1}$ is chosen at random, split evenly into two new subsets, thereby increasing the number of groupings. The goal is to minimize the expected cost associated with the partition configuration at each time point $t$, which includes both the cost associated with splitting and the cost associated with the configuration at time $t$. This optimization can be rephrased as a classic stochastic control issue, for which we suggest an efficient approximation technique, implementing a discrete-state model with increasing dimensions. The proposed approximation technique outperforms traditional methods, such as linear programming, by significantly reducing computational time and efficiency.

In the context of chess, a superior player is defined as someone with a positive Skill Level (SL), while their opponents are classified as having a negative SL. Given these definitions, the objective of this research is to develop a method to calculate a player's SL based on their game outcomes, with the goal of facilitating accurate predictions of match results. To achieve this, the study proposes an iterative algorithm for SL calculation, along with two initial value methods that exploit properties of the logistic map, offering a theoretical framework for SL determination. The study also presents empirical results derived from actual match data, which indicate that the SL values derived from this method correlate strongly with those calculated using more conventional methods, while also revealing that the SL values determined in this study correspond closely to those of a player's rating (R), with the ratio of SL to R for superior players found to be approximately 10 times larger in this context. Furthermore, the study shows that the SL values are more finely graded than the R values, with those of the top players exhibiting a notably tighter distribution. Finally, the study demonstrates that, in contrast to conventional rating systems, the SL values fail to capture any trends or patterns in players' game histories.

a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The paper provides information about the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The investigation of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state, rather than through the $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ ground state, can be performed through a unique coincidence measurement of three alpha particles. The paper outlines a specific method to detect this direct decay and discusses the associated background removal techniques. The detection efficiency and statistical accuracy of the experiment are also discussed in detail. The paper presents the first experimental measurement of the direct decay probability of the Hoyle state by measuring the number of three-in-one alpha particle decay events and calculating the transition probability to the ground state of $^{12}\mathrm{C}$. The measurement shows a 13 times higher decay probability in the direct path compared to previously detected indirect pathways. The paper concludes by discussing its implications on our understanding of the atomic structure of the Hoyle state.

The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds in 2D, an intrinsic fracture energy exists, independent of the crack speed, and is influenced by the material's nonlinear elastic response. An inherent oscillation pattern was found in 2D fractures, resulting from an interplay between a crack's rapid propagation and a material's dissipation properties. Research has also demonstrated that in 2D fractures with a lack of dissipation, a singular point exists, characterized by an infinitely high energy release rate, marking the transition from a stable to an unstable crack state. In 3D fracture, a distinct feature is the alignment of cracks with the shortest path, which is largely a result of the self-force generated during high-speed propagation. Research has addressed the influence of a crack's speed on its direction, and revealed that in 3D, an intrinsic fracture energy exists, unaffected by the crack speed. Unlike 2D, a dissipation-dominated energy contribution in 3D determines the crack speed and an intrinsic fracture energy. Research has further focused on 3D crack branching and termination, and has shown that in 3D, a crack's branch point distance can be accurately predicted, even at speeds where the material exhibits nonlinear elastic response.

However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution remains challenging due to limitations imposed by measurement technology.  As a result, modeling becomes a necessary tool to assist engineers in process design.  This paper presents a detailed modeling approach that utilizes an adaptive grid refinement technique to precisely capture temperature fluctuations at every point in time during heat transfer in a cylindrical reactor.  This heat transfer model is based on an Eulerian volume element framework, where both the fluid and solid phases are represented.  Furthermore, the model accounts for heat conduction in both phases as well as heat transfer resulting from both axial and radial dispersion processes.  All model coefficients and their effects are systematically examined.  Comparison of the modeled temperature profiles with actual temperature measurements confirms that the proposed model accurately predicts temperature distributions, thereby establishing its potential as a reliable tool for process design and optimization.

SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. To address this need, we have developed an open-access web platform providing real-time analysis of the pandemic's progression based on non-parametric statistical methods. The core functionality of the site revolves around comparing two groups - cases with a known exposure history and those without such history - to determine their infection risk disparity. Consequently, users can obtain insights into the virus transmission likelihood associated with specific demographic and geographical variables, thereby gaining better control over risk assessment and decision-making.

During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection.

Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be detected as an energetic gamma-ray signal. We examine three methods to detect this signal, specifically diffuse background detection, correlated anisotropy measurement, and the search for spatially localized sources. To determine the detectability of this background, we created advanced simulations accounting for foreground radiation, instrumentation limitations, and the likelihood of detecting PBHs of varying masses and ages. Based on these simulations, we found that the future AMIDEA X-Linear survey is likely to detect the cosmic background of Hawking radiation if it occurs from PBHs weighing approximately 10^16-10^19 grams and accounts for about 1% of the total density. Conversely, the future CMB-S4 experiment might be able to detect this background under more restrictive conditions, specifically for PBHs weighing around 10^16-10^17 grams and representing less than 1% of the total density. We found that the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes will likely be detectable by both surveys unless produced by extremely light PBHs (approximately 10^9-10^11 grams) making up the entire density.

is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly for solving optimization problems. The proposed computation model is based on the Turing machine with some essential extensions, including unbounded parallel memory access and arbitrary size arithmetic operations. In this framework, each operation can be either a memory access or an arithmetic operation. The model's time complexity is measured by the number of operations and is denoted as $t_{\mathrm{op}}$. Additionally, the model allows for a specified number of free operations, up to a given limit, without affecting the overall time complexity. The research demonstrates that this foundation provides a uniform and consistent approach to complexity theory, offering a more accurate and flexible toolset for analyzing algorithmic solutions. Specifically, it shows that problems with different input sizes have the same complexity, and that algorithms can be easily modified to work with different input sizes while maintaining the same complexity. Additionally, the research provides more precise and informative complexity results for well-known problems, such as sorting and finding the closest pair in a set of points.

high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break up and scatter in the magnetic field of the interstellar medium. A detailed study of these halos can provide valuable insights into the conditions of the medium and the properties of the particles that created them. Due to their diffuse nature and distant location, it's challenging to study these halos directly. However, researchers can examine nearby clouds and compare the results with observations of the more distant, brighter pulsar halos around the Sun. In this study, a multi-frequency study of the Flamingos supernova remnant using the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the HESS TeV gamma-ray telescope was conducted to explore the interaction between a shock front and particles from a pulsar. Despite extensive searches, no pulsar halo was found within the remnant. A simulation based on the magnetic field and temperature in the remnant indicated that any pulsar halo would be obscured by the supernova remnant's shock front. This suggests that the lack of a pulsar halo within the remnant means the responsible pulsar cannot be seen, and its curvature could be greater than expected. As a result, the distance to the pulsar is likely much greater, and its contribution to the local cosmic ray density is minimal.

holes can provide a direct look into the black hole activity in the early universe. Specifically, misaligned jet emissions from these ancient black holes can give a full picture of how they grew and how they lit up the surrounding space. A problem in studying these ancient black holes is the lack of complete information - only partially observed emissions from certain events are available. To better understand these ancient black holes, researchers need to find a way to use all available information. To tackle this challenge, a new mathematical framework is developed, allowing it to incorporate any amount of data and adjust for possible biases in observations. Using this new framework, researchers can better understand how often and how strong jet emissions were during certain periods of black hole growth. To better account for possible biases, the framework includes a new formula that helps to level out any unevenness in observations. To apply this new framework, researchers can use all available data - both direct and indirect emissions evidence. Studies using this new framework show that there may have been at least a tenfold increase in black hole activity during peak growth periods compared to what was previously thought. Furthermore, researchers found that jet emissions were likely stronger and more frequent during black hole activity than the current evidence shows. To further study black hole activity, researchers need to find a way to include possible biases in observations and continue to gather more complete data on ancient black holes.

Although it may seem counter-intuitive at first, the second law relies on two critical principles from statistical mechanics: the non-violation of detailed balance and time reversal invariance of the transition rates. This underlying framework provides valuable insights into the underlying dynamics of the dissipative systems. In this research, we demonstrate how these transition rate principles enable dissipation and entropy production through a simple mean-field approach applicable to extensive systems. Our results also show that the entropy production is bounded by a measure derived from the relative entropy, known as the relative entropy production. This research contributes to the growing body of literature bridging microscopic and macroscopic phenomena, and it paves the way for further extensions to more complex systems like open systems and systems with multiple components.

Building upon this concept, we have also devised a straightforward method to create maximum probabilistic protocols, which achieves the maximum possible outcome probability in relation to a specific measurement outcome. the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains a relatively small amount of mass per year, typically no more than 10 to the minus 3 solar masses. However, this low-mass rate also means that less-strong magnetic fields are required to produce the high-velocity jets. For more rapid mass accumulation rates, the high-velocity jets appear later and at lower velocities. Another key finding is that rapid protostar growth in strongly magnetized clouds can lead to jet deceleration early on, which might explain some observed phenomena. The study suggests that strong magnetic fields and low mass accumulation rates are necessary for the early formation of high-velocity jets. As the protostar gains more mass per year, either due to an increase in accretion rate or age, the magnetic field's influence on jet velocity likely shifts from supporting high velocities to potentially limiting them.

we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories. For instance, recognizing a car or a fire engine, regardless of its make or model, falls under this category. Research in category-level perception has been conducted, with most developments centered around computer vision. In contrast, we explore the feasibility of achieving this capability using audio sensors, given their widespread presence and capabilities. To this end, we introduce a framework allowing an agent to learn category-level insights by combining both local and global understanding of their environment, acquired through the collection and sharing of audio data. In the context of a fire monitoring simulation, our framework proves effective in allowing fire engines to effectively locate and identify fires, even when their sensors have limited visibility due to obstacles. Moreover, our results show that fire engines can still successfully locate and access fires, even when their access to the full environment is restricted and when other agents are using similar sensing strategies. This highlights the importance of balancing local and global understanding in fire monitoring and suggests potential applications in other category-level perception tasks.

, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, we explore its significance and importance, particularly in simulating the sound of bodies hitting the ground. Through physical modeling, we generate a mathematical representation of ground sound, leading to the development of a sampled synthesis approach for modeling ground sound interactions. By applying this model to a falling steel ball, we observed that ground sound can be substantial and in some cases, even louder than the sound produced by the object itself. Furthermore, when the object hits the ground, the ground sound can be extremely loud, exceeding the object's sound and even producing transient hearing loss. Our modeled ground sound can be divided into three components: the sound of the object's base, the sound of the object's sides, and the sound produced by the object's inertia, which is a phenomenon previously unreported in the literature.

This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many researchers to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing belief, our study reveals a new family of "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs, which are based on correlations that deviate from perfection. This is achieved using a novel method of constructing private states, which were previously overlooked in research. The private states utilized in our work originate from single copies of the quantum state $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2+\sqrt{3}}}|00\rangle + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2-\sqrt{3}}}|11\rangle$. A shared basis can be established by measuring this state in the Bell basis, resulting in outcomes that closely resemble the perfect correlations produced by stabilizer states, but with an error that is strictly greater than zero and less than one. This leads to a family of "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs that are based on such correlations. has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Although the core concepts of calculus are universally based on a common set of principles, there has been a variety of interpretations regarding their meaning. Historically, Augustus De Morgan developed a method to translate mathematical operations into algebraic forms, which has become a widely accepted approach to interpreting calculus. However, this method has been found to yield distinct formulations for calculus operations, which implies that they are inherently different. Conversely, a more recent approach known as the algebraic differentiation technique suggests that calculus operations have a common foundation. By applying the traditional method and the algebraic differentiation technique to the core concepts of calculus, we have found that they produce equivalent results, which confirms that these operations have a common foundation. Moreover, the results of the algebraic differentiation technique provide a clearer understanding of the inverse operations, which has significant implications for the development of calculus. Additionally, the findings of our study suggest that the most common interpretations of calculus are based on a common set of principles, which are expressed through the formulations of De Morgan.

This allows us to assess the theoretical accuracy of 3PCF observations, potentially limiting their usefulness if the required higher-order corrections are significant. Under typical cosmological conditions and for galaxies at redshift z=1.5, we find that 3PCF measurements are heavily influenced by quartic terms in the bias. On the other hand, although the 3PCF should offer improved precision, it is the 3PCF that is best suited to accurately validating the EFT approach to analyzing large scale structure.

We delve into the concept of redundancy among association rules from a theoretical perspective. Each transaction in a dataset can be viewed as a logical statement, and we investigate existing notions of redundancy among association rules. We explore alternative definitions of redundancy and introduce new characterizations, highlighting relationships between these concepts. We demonstrate that two distinct notions of redundancy exist, differing in how full-confidence implications are treated. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, acting as a source of photons, which can then interact either with other photons or with hadrons. Specifically, ultrarelativistic nuclei give rise to a significant number of photons with low energies, making them susceptible to being absorbed by targets, often resulting in limits being imposed on photon-nucleon interactions at low energies. In contrast, within the context of ultrarelativistic nuclear collisions, energy densities are high enough to enable effective photon production from both electric and magnetic fields in a dense QED plasma. As a result, electromagnetic phenomena play a crucial role, particularly in collisions at the HADRON collider where intense electromagnetic fields are produced. In this review, the current state of electromagnetic phenomena is discussed, with a focus on their occurrence in strong electromagnetic fields present in heavy ion collisions. This includes observations of direct photon production, radiation from charged particles, and electromagnetic phenomena, with a comprehensive examination of recent data from the LHC.

The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a broad category of deep learning models known as LeNet. The proposed system involves the development of innovative algorithms that significantly reduce computational cost, from exponential to linear complexity, based on the specific type of model being used. A comprehensive evaluation of DataScope's performance has been conducted using datasets from image classification, such as the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, which revealed valuable insights into the impact of data quality on the accuracy and fairness of the model. intelligence (AI) systems capable of performing significantly better than their human counterparts. In this context, the importance of question-answering (QA) systems becomes evident, given their potential to learn from a range of questions, unlike other existing AI applications that typically focus a single task. By learning from these diverse queries, a QA system can acquire knowledge comparable to that of a human. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework, called Quadra, which facilitates the acquisition of multi-modal knowledge from a range of questions and answers. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, highlighting its potential to construct accurate knowledge graphs and validate knowledge through a combination of semantic analysis and numerical evaluation.

cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant assets. After excluding unusually large price fluctuations, the correlations between cryptocurrency prices and those of its component assets remain consistent throughout. Notably, the correlations between cryptocurrency prices and component asset prices do not differ significantly from their individual autoregressive correlations, suggesting that the prices of major cryptocurrencies are effectively isolated from their underlying component assets' prices. Moreover, the correlations between cryptocurrency prices and component asset prices do not anticipate future price shifts in cryptocurrencies, undermining the notion that they can be utilized as early indicators. Ultimately, the correlations between cryptocurrency prices and component asset prices are likely influenced by general market trends rather than the specific characteristics of the component assets themselves.

Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of tackling the complex "visual question answering" (VQA) challenge. However, the reliance of existing gradient-based optimization methods on raw data for gradient updates can impede performance and lead to overfitting due to their inefficiency in exploiting global structure. Moreover, the constraint of limited available data hinders the development of effective VQA models. In an effort to address these issues, this paper proposes an innovative method called Region-based Gradient-based Optimization (RGO). RGO involves partitioning the gradient across regions and incorporating external knowledge to facilitate efficient backpropagation. We also introduce an adaptive optimization approach based on region-based mean squared errors (MSE). We evaluate the effectiveness of RGO by implementing it on multiple state-of-the-art VQA models and observe significant performance enhancements as well as improved generalization capabilities.

graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. We pinpoint two inefficient aspects: the repeated search for neighbors in each layer, resulting in distorted spatial structure, and the use of a soft non-linearity function, diminishing gradient propagation. To address these issues, we propose Efficient Graph Convolutional Networks (EffGCNs), comprising two optimizations. Firstly, we utilize a binary mask to retain spatial structure integrity through batch-normalized spatial filtering. Secondly, we employ a hard non-linearity function in the form of a ReLU activation function to expedite gradient propagation. Experimental evaluations on multiple point cloud datasets demonstrate the computational efficiency and performance superiority of EffGCNs, particularly in inference time and model parameter complexity. The source code is available at https://github.com/Al-Assim/EffGCNs.

Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the randomness inherent to statistical samples but also possible inaccuracies in the input data and approximations used. To effectively assess the dependences predicted by NNs on fundamental physical parameters, we propose a novel approach called "p-mesh refinement." This technique is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of physical problems described by partial differential equations. In this study, we utilize the p-mesh refinement method to investigate the flow of viscous fluids described by the Navier-Stokes equations in various scenarios. Our analysis demonstrates how background noise, inaccuracies in input data, and approximations affect NN predictions for the drag force exerted on an immersed object. Furthermore, we show that these errors can be significantly reduced, often below the threshold of numerical precision, by utilizing the p-mesh refinement method to validate the NN predictions. Based on these findings, we recommend adopting the p-mesh refinement method as a reliable means of validating NN-based predictions in physics and engineering applications.

semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical calculations, researchers investigated the behavior of spin polarization within the prototype ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayer, which has an in-plane magnetization orientation. Their investigation reveals that this ferromagnetic bilayer displays a rich pattern of spin texture within its uppermost valence bands, which arises from two distinct types of spin canting resulting in non-zero spin torques. One type of canted spin structure, characterized by spins aligned perpendicular to each other, forms within layers, while the other, involving spins twisted around their common axis, develops within interlayer bonds. Both types of canted spins cause a spin drift directed perpendicular to the drift velocity, which in turn generates a spin torque. Researchers observed a significant drift velocity when considering only the component of spin torque related to the spin drift. Conversely, a spin drift velocity opposed to that produced by CrI$_3$ monolayers is generated by the component of spin torque related to the spin twist. Additionally, researchers found that this ferromagnetic bilayer exhibits a notable response to spin transfer, which suggests its potential for use in spin transfer torque devices and could also enable the manipulation of spin drift in magnetic semiconductors via spin transfer.

Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making the Braking Law a crucial aspect. Additionally to the angular momentum loss due to the coupling with a magnetic dynamo in a solar-type star, a possible supplementary factor could be the removal of its coronal plasma through radiative winds, known as the "coronal evaporation effect". This process might have an insignificant impact on angular momentum loss but could play a significant role in mass loss. To further investigate this phenomenon, we conducted a study using 3D MHD simulations that included a couple representing the interaction between the star's interior and its exterior. This coupling consisted of a viscous coupling factor of 0.1 and a coupling parameter for the interaction between the star's interior and its exterior as 0.7. Upon observing the results, we noticed that both the magnetic and non-magnetic winds present at the star's surface experience significant mass loss. This leads to a reduction in the effect of the magnetic interaction by as much as 50% due to the "coronal evaporation effect". As a result, we need a more complex model that includes both the magnetic interaction and the "coronal evaporation effect" in order to accurately explain the observed slowdown of a solar-type star's rotation.

A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often requires less storage and runs faster. A different option is the Bloomier filter, a structure that combines Bloom filters with hash tables for efficient in-memory storage. A recent innovation is the Bloomier filter's updated incarnation along with novel filter variants that can be built using shared memory. These updates offer improved performance and reduced memory usage compared to standard Bloom filters. A primary challenge lies in allowing multiple threads to safely access and manage the filter without interfering with each other's operations. A shared memory solution is proposed that addresses this issue by implementing synchronization mechanisms to guarantee reliable performance and minimal overhead. A test suite verifies the updated code's correct functioning and compares the updated filters with their single-threaded counterparts along with cuckoo filters. Results indicate that the updated shared memory Bloomier filter implementation yields significant performance gains in several test scenarios, notably in preventing false positives and removing elements from the filter. Furthermore, these improvements translate to considerable time savings and storage reductions, showcasing the updated shared memory Bloomier filter as a high-performance and efficient solution.

Neural Networks (CNNs) are key components in modern deep learning architectures, but they demand significant computational resources and have substantial energy consumption. This paper focuses on estimating the energy cost of CNNs by evaluating various activation functions, which are pivotal in determining both computational complexity and memory requirements. Our study comprehends both theoretical and practical aspects, encompassing analysis of energy-efficient properties and hands-on experiments on embedded hardware. The findings reveal that, while certain sophisticated activation functions appear computationally efficient, they actually incur substantial memory usage and energy expenses due to storage needs. In contrast, simpler functions like ReLU or Softplus exhibit lower energy costs despite their computational complexity. Moreover, we propose an energy-efficient custom implementation for these functions, which yields substantial energy savings in practice. The research was conducted on the Raspberry Pi 4B and NVIDIA Jetson TX2, and showcases that with both hardware and software optimizations, energy-efficient deep learning models can be effectively deployed on embedded devices.

These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches can be utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of local independence, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance, or applying continuous data methods to the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances. These clustering methods vary conceptually and cannot easily be compared theoretically. To address this, we conduct an in-depth comparative analysis through simulation studies grounded in models for species distribution to evaluate their respective performances. 

This study assesses the effectiveness of these clustering methods using metrics such as the widely used Wilks' C metric divided by its standard error, information criteria like the Bayesian information criterion, and cross-entropy, in addition to visually evaluating the clustering of species using spatial maps and comparing these to independently grouped species based on DNA analysis. 

Results indicate that the performance of these clustering approaches depends both on the true cluster structure and the number of clusters present. Generally, multi-component mixture models and hierarchical clustering exhibit higher success rates compared to the other methods examined. These findings suggest potential improvements in the application of these clustering methods in the analysis of presence-absence data.

For complex decision functions that have been developed using machine learning techniques, validating their robustness in high-stakes environments can be a significant challenge. One potential solution involves utilizing robustness-testing tools to simulate and identify potential weaknesses. By incorporating these tools into machine learning development, researchers can test the robustness of their models more effectively. Our research provides an overview of the current state of robustness testing, presents a groundbreaking approach, and demonstrates its effectiveness in identifying potential vulnerabilities of decision functions that have been developed using machine learning techniques.

Despite its promise, a key challenge lies in finding a reliable method for verifying the correctness of CPT algorithms, particularly those defined by random choices. This fundamental issue of verifying CPT algorithms at an algorithmic level is the primary focus of our research. We identify a key condition for reliable verification of CPT algorithms and propose a method to design computationally efficient, reliable indicators for a wide range of CPT-identifiable problems. Our research reveals that each problem recognizable within CPT is characterized by a specific set of computable indices that can be associated with its corresponding computation process. We also demonstrate that these indices can be efficiently calculated and provide reliable indicators, which facilitate efficient testing of whether a given problem's index corresponds to an efficient computation process. We provide a concrete example of a CPT-recognizable problem, along with an efficient indicator that can be used to verify whether a given algorithm is likely to produce an answer within a specified time limit. We also offer an efficient method for generating a set of computationally efficient, reliable indicators for a CPT-recognizable problem and provide a probabilistic guarantee that this set will efficiently determine the correct computation process for that problem. We propose a probabilistic algorithm that can be used to verify whether a given algorithm is likely to produce an answer

a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, non-identical integers $k, l, m$, where $k > l$, and $m > n$, that fulfill the following condition: for each $i$, $x_{i \mod 2}$ equals $1 - x_{(i+1) \mod 2}$ and $x_{(i+1) \mod 2}$ equals $1-x_i$. This paper proves all possible n-tuples $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ are cyclic when $n$ equals 3 or 5. It was discovered that any possible n-tuple is not cyclic when $n$ equals 7 or 3, due to a particular function, $f(x)$, being defined as $f(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = 1-x_2+ \ldots + (-1)^{n+1} \ldots + x_n$, which results in a value equal to $\frac{1}{2}$. This led to concluding all n-tuples are not cyclic when $n$ equals 7.

graph data analysis systems.  Graph-based machine learning has made notable advancements recently, but detecting events in evolving networks remains an challenging area.  Current methods focus on either fixed-size events in static graphs or entire network trajectories, but not on defined events within dynamic graphs.  This work introduces a new approach, NEME, which can identify specified events in arbitrary-sized dynamic graphs.  Event definitions are represented by logical combinations of node properties in a colored graph, and NEme accurately detects these events by utilizing node attributes in the Vertex Identification Algorithm.  This approach supports arbitrary-node events in any dynamic graph and is adaptable to changing event definitions.  Additionally, NEme detects events at a specific time frame, accounts for node attributes' temporal properties, and handles asynchronous events.  This method is further validated by experimental results showing its efficiency and accuracy compared to alternative methods for detecting events in dynamic graphs.

In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explanations and the reliability of AI systems, particularly in three key aspects: (1) the trust that stakeholders has in these systems, (2) the accuracy of results produced by the systems, and (3) the accountability of these systems. The process of polyp characterization involves examining histological slides to identify specific molecular markers, a time-consuming task that can be streamlined by applying deep learning technology. Particularly challenging in this domain are deep learning models requiring access to vast amounts of labeled data to optimize their performance, a scenario presenting particular challenges when dealing with limited or diverse datasets of histological slides. In response to these obstacles, the development of data-driven methods that can leverage existing knowledge to enhance performance without compromising quality has become a priority. To that end, a novel approach, known as Semi-Supervised Convolutional Neural Networks (SS-FCL), has been designed to efficiently train deep learning models using limited datasets and existing knowledge derived from various sources. By incorporating domain adaptation and semi-supervised learning strategies, SS-FCL allows for the refinement of models using labeled data, while also leveraging unlabeled data and domain-specific knowledge to improve performance. By applying SS-FCL to the task of polyp characterization, a more efficient and effective deep learning model has been developed, demonstrating improved accuracy and efficiency in characterizing colorectal polyps, while also addressing the limitations of data scarcity and heterogeneity.

our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source outcomes can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source outcome is measured relative to its prior knowledge, reflected by the adversary's discrimination measure. Our central finding establishes that, under certain conditions, achieving nearly optimal compression with low error rates is possible only if a related function of the adversary's discrimination measure meets specific lower limits. These limits dictate the minimum rate needed to keep error rates below a specified threshold, even when the adversary's discrimination measure is extremely low. Conversely, our analysis also determines a condition under which this important result no longer holds. To validate these conclusions, specific families of confusion graphs have been created and analyzed. These examples provide precise insights into how source coding rates and error rates interact, particularly in cases where an adversary's situation is particularly favorable. Furthermore, our research offers a novel approach for finding optimal confusion graphs, as existing methods were limited in their ability to design such graphs under detailed compression requirements. Our investigation's tools and techniques can now be applied to a broader range of coding problems, equipped with this deeper understanding.

This approach utilizes a quantum circuit to generate an approximate solution based on an initial perturbed state, with an alternating iterative process that integrates both classical and quantum components to produce successive solutions.  This paper offers an in-depth analysis of the quantum circuit's propensity to produce optimal solutions.  Under specific conditions, for a particular class of problems known as constraint satisfaction problems, it has been proven that the quality of the solution produced by a particular QAOA variant depends on variables that represent the depth of the circuit and the structural characteristics of the problem, which provides valuable insight into the performance of this algorithm for such problems.  This research provides a critical examination of the influence of the number of qubits and variables in the problem and the length of a specific ancillary path on the circuit's behavior.  Additionally, this study presents an expanded explanation of a specific variant of the QAOA, known as the variational hybrid quantum-classical optimization algorithm, which incorporates both classical and quantum components to produce improved solutions.  It has been found that this variant of the QAOA can produce solutions of equivalent or higher quality using fewer qubits and variables than alternative methods.

This method incorporates diffusion and excitation variables into a generalized approach for analyzing spatial light spectra. By studying a canonical semiconductor system consisting of a p-i-n structure within a Fabry-Perot cavity, we have conducted detailed simulations to identify and validate critical parameters influencing photoluminescence patterns, including diffusion coefficients, excitation intensity, energy gap, and built-in potential. By introducing a measure of energy disparity, $\Delta E$, we derive a generalized Gibbs form for the stationary distribution, accommodating any energy function that remains finite under normalization. Furthermore, we show that the system's stationary probability is directly proportional to $e^{-\beta \langle \Delta E \rangle _\mathcal P}$, where $\mathcal P$ represents the probability measure. Notably, this expression is akin to the traditional expression $e^{-\beta E}$ employed in equilibrium statistical mechanics, where $\mathcal P$ is replaced by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis also encompasses systems undergoing continuous processes and reveals that the energy disparity, modulated by the system's dynamics, plays a pivotal role in determining the system's stationary characteristics.

-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris and its survival around the planet a topic of ongoing research. Our investigation delves into high-resolution spectra obtained through the HIRES instrument on Magellan, which yield unambiguous evidence of water vapor in the upper atmosphere of K2-22b. By modeling the planet's atmospheric structure as a warm, expanding atmosphere surrounded by a cooling gas cloud, we are able to explain the observed spectral features and the decline in transit depths and changes in wavelength shifts. Our atmospheric model suggests that the planet has an inflated radius due to a substantial atmosphere primarily composed of water and that this atmosphere is being continuously eroded by the solar wind, with new material being generated in a cometary envelope. Furthermore, we find that the planet's core is composed of a rock-like substance. By modeling the planet's mass loss, we find that a significant portion of its mass has been lost over its lifetime, which in turn affects its heat budget and potential habitability.

C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this tool facilitates data preparation, feature engineering, and other data transformation operations. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple VS projects that can be easily installed as a NuGet package. At its core, Daany utilizes the DataFrame data structure, complemented by data science and linear algebra capabilities, including time series decomposition (SSA, STL, ARIMA) and optimization methods (SGD). The library also integrates matrix and vector operations, as well as data plotting functionality. Daany's implementation bears similarities to Python's Pandas library.

Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation. The comparative study involves three scenarios: the MHD-AEPIC model, MHD simulations paired with fixed embedded PIC regions, and full PIC simulations. The examination of reconnection rates, magnetic island spacings, and ion dynamics within these scenarios indicates that the MHD-AEPIC model produces comparable results to those of full PIC simulations, with notable improvements over fixed embedded PIC simulations in terms of accuracy. The implementation of adaptive embedded PIC regions enhances computational efficiency, with potential to make more complex, three-dimensional kinetic simulations feasible via the MHD-AEPIC model.
